layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in various chloride-containing environments, and it was found that pitting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: to chloride solutions (1). Data have also been presented

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indicating that above room temperature, the beneficial

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: effects of molybdenum on resistance to pitting may

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: May 1973

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 18% chromium steels containing 0-5% Mo. These mea-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: surements were made in 1M NaCl and 1M NaBr over

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a temperature range from 1° to 70°C. Concurrently,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: some exposure tests were performed in various media

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: containing chlorides or bromides.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Experimental

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The experimental alloys were produced by induc-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion-melting in an argon atmosphere using the split-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: heat technique. By this technique, the base composi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion was melted and part of the melt was poured off to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: produce an ingot. To the balance of the melt, the re-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: quired molybdenum addition was made and the next

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ingot was cast. This process was repeated until the de-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sired compositions were cast. By this procedure, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: impurity levels were held nearly constant within each

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: series. The compositions of the steels produced are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: given in Table I.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The resulting ingots were hot-forged and hot-rolled

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to 0.76 cm thick strips and then cold-rolled to 0.38 cm

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thickness. All strips were given a 1-hr anneal at 815°C

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and water-quenched before the test specimens were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prepared.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The electrodes for the potentiodynamic studies were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mounted in epoxy plastic with a single exposed sur-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: face parallel to the rolling plane. Electrical contact

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was made by soft-soldering a nickel wire to the back

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the electrode. Contact between the solder or lead

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: wire and the electrolyte was excluded by the plastic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and glass tube. The 0.5 by 0.6 cm exposed surface was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: polished by using standard metallographic techniques,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: finishing with a distilled water slurry of 0.3μ alumina.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The edges of the electrode were masked with clear

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Glyptal varnish to prevent crevice corrosion.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The coupons for the exposure tests, 2.5 by 2.5 by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 0.3 cm, were surface ground and then polished through

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: No. 600 wet silicon carbide paper. They were solvent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: degreased and rinsed in methanol before exposure.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The potentiodynamic scanning experiments were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: performed using standard equipment and techniques

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The platinum auxiliary electrode was isolated from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the test solution by means of a glass frit. The solution

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: used was nitrogen-saturated 1.0M NaCl or 1.0M NaBr.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: All potential measurements were made using a satu-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rated calomel reference electrode. The scans were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: started at —0.7V and continued in the noble direction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at 200 mV/hr. The temperature was controlled within

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ±0.5°C of the reported temperature. Below room

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: temperature an ice bath was used, while the elevated

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: temperatures were maintained by a heating mantle

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and temperature controller.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Results and Discussion

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A typical pitting potential determination is shown in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Fig. 1. It can be seen that the current rise correspond-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ing to pitting is extremely sharp. This was true at all

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: temperatures investigated. It can also be seen that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: very short pulses of current were sometimes observed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as the pitting potential was approached. As discussed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: previously (4), these pulses correspond to formation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of very tiny pits that do not propagate if the potential

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: scan is stopped below the pitting potential for time

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: periods up to 24 hr.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The effect of variation in the rate of potential scan

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was checked for the 18% Cr-2% Mo alloy (Table II).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Table I. Compositions of steels tested

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (a) NA = not analyzed, but assumed to be in the range of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: series.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Fig. 1. Polarization curve obtained on scanning a masked electrode

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of alloy 4354D (3.5% Mo at 200 mV/hr in nitrogen-saturated 1.0M

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: NaCl at 70°C).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: No significant difference in pitting potential was ob-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tained when the scan rate was increased from 200 to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2000 mV/hr. This is in contrast to results obtained in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: previous study of an 18% Cr-14% Ni-3% Mo aus-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tenitic steel (4). This austenitic steel showed a signifi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cant decrease in pitting potential as scan rate increased.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In general, it has been observed that pitting potentials

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of ferritic steels are less affected by variations in ex-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perimental conditions than are pitting potentials of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: austenitic steels of similar chromium and molybdenum

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: content.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: After each run, the electrode was examined under

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the microscope. Only if well-developed pits, away from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the masked edges, were present was a run accepted

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as valid. In many cases, there was simultaneous attack

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at the edges where crevices may have existed, but this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was disregarded if distinct pits were visible. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: crevice attack was more likely to occur as the test

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: temperature decreased. At 70°C, most electrodes were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: free of any crevice attack, while at 1°C, most elec-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: trodes suffered crevice attack as well as pitting. This

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: effect may be partially a result of the physical proper-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ties of the Glyptal mask, which tended to be brittle

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at low temperatures.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: When pitting occurred, a large number of pits were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: usually found. If the scan was stopped at this point,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: but without the potentiostat switched off, the pits

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: would continue to grow until the electrode was de-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stroyed.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Results of the tests in 1M NaCl are shown in Fig. 2.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: While temperature had a very large effect on pitting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: potentials of these alloys, it is striking that the effect

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of molybdenum was nearly the same at each of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: test temperatures. Thus, over the temperature range

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: studied, molybdenum exerts a definite beneficial effect

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on pitting potentials. Note that an increase in the pit-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ting potential in the noble direction corresponds to an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: increase in resistance to pitting corrosion. However,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the pitting potentials of the 4.7% Mo alloy did tend to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be lower than those observed for the 3.5% Mo steel.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Since this difference was observed at each temperature,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it appears to be a true effect and not the result of ex-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perimental variation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A similar tendency for a maximum in pitting poten-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tial to occur at intermediate molybdenum content was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also observed for an austenitic stainless steel series

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (4). This behavior in the austenitic series was attri-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: steels, a second phase also occurs in the high molyb-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: denum steels. According to the work of McMullin et al.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (5), at 815°C, this phase is chi, a compound contain-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ing about 25% Mo, 18% Cr, and the balance iron. Ac-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cording to the phase diagram, at 815°C the maximum

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: solubility of molybdenum is about 3.5% in 18% Cr-Fe

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (5). Thus, the 4.7% Mo alloy does not have any more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: molybdenum dissolved in the matrix than does the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3.5% Mo alloy. Examination of the microstructures

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the steels annealed at 815°C indicated that a very

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: small amount of chi was present in the 3.5% Mo steel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and a large amount in the 4.7% Mo steel (Fig. 3).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Therefore, it is concluded that the failure of the 4.7%

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Mo alloy to exhibit a higher pitting potential than the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3.5% Mo steel is a consequence of the phase constitu-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion of the alloys. The slight decrease in pitting poten-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tial that was apparently observed could either indi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cate that chi itseif is not as resistant as the matrix to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pitting or that the chi-ferrite interface forms preferen-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tial pitting sites. In any event, the decrease in pitting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: potential of the 4.7% Mo steel as compared to the 3.5%

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Mo steel was too small to be of practical significance.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In an effort to avoid the chi phase, the three alloys

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with the highest molybdenum content were annealed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at 980°C and water-quenched. Microscopic examina-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion confirmed that all of these steels did not contain

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: appreciable chi after treatment. However, the pitting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: potentials found in 1.0M NaCl at 25°C were consider-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ably reduced by the 980°C treatment (Table III).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: It is known that this heat-treatment also sensitizes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: these steels to intergranular corrosion (6). It is thought

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that the intergranular corrosion is the result of precip-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: itation of carbides and nitrides rich in chromium and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: molybdenum, causing depletion of the adjacent matrix

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (7). Thus, it is to be expected that steels heat-treated

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: so as to be sensitive to intergranular corrosion would

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Fig. 3. Structure (islands of chi in a ferrite matrix) of the 18%

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cr-5% Mo alloy (4354E) annealed 1 hr at 815°C and water-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: quenched; 500×.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be more susceptible to pitting corrosion than would

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: properly annealed steels, as was recently reported for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 26% Cr ferritic alloys (8). A similar effect has been

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: observed for austenitic stainless steels exposed in ferric

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: chloride (9).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The foregoing results lead to the conclusion that the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: maximum useful molybdenum content of 18% Cr steels

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: containing the usual amounts of interstitial elements

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and not fully stabilized is about 3.5%. Steels fully

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stabilized by titanium or columbium additions that tie

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: up all carbon and nitrogen, or steels of such low inter-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stitial content that carbides or nitrides do not precipi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tate, could be annealed at high enough temperatures

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to dissolve chi without suffering chromium depletion

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: because of carbide or nitride precipitation. In this case,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: larger molybdenum additions can contribute to cor-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rosion resistance, as was demonstrated in work on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: high-purity 25% Cr steels containing up to 5% Mo

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In order to demonstrate that titanium stabilization

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tization to intergranular corrosion as a result of ex-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: can prevent loss of pitting resistance as well as sensi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: posure to high temperatures, the pitting potential of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an 18% Cr-2% Mo-0.5% Ti alloy was determined as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a function of heat-treatment. It was found (Table IV)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that, as expected, heat-treatment at temperatures up

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to 1035°C had no deleterious effect on pitting poten-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tial. In fact, after treatment at 1035°C, the pitting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: potential was more noble than it was after the normal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: annèal at 815°C. It was also noted that the titanium-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: containing alloy had a more noble pitting potential

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: than the titanium-free alloy under the same conditions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Earlier work with this alloy at 25°C also indicated

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that titanium was beneficial to pitting resistance (11).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Pitting potentials measured in 1M NaBr varied with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: composition in the same way as in 1M NaCl (Fig. 4).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Pitting potentials were more noble in NaBr, especially

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at higher temperatures. The beneficial effect of molyb-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: denum additions on pitting potentials of this series of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: steels in NaBr is just as clearly defined as it is in NaCl.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The pitting potentials measured in 1M NaCl and in 1M

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: NaBr at 25°C indicate that all the steels studied

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: should be subject to pitting in 0.33M FeCl3, 0.5M CuCl2,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and 0.33M FeBr3 solutions. Exposure tests did indeed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: show pitting of all the test steels in these solutions at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 25°C (Table V). In all cases, the rate of attack de-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: creased with increasing molybdenum content up to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3.5%. The behavior of the 4.7% Mo steel was erratic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in these solutions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Exposure tests were also performed in less aggres-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sive media at 90°C (Table VI). In both solutions, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: molybdenum-free steel was severely pitted, while the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: steels containing molybdenum were attacked only very

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: slightly or not at all. These exposure test results were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in good qualitative agreement with the pitting poten-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tial results.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Table V. Results of exposure tests in acidified halide salts at 25°C

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: As a result of the polarization measurements, it is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clear that molybdenum has a beneficial effect on pitting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: potentials in 1M NaCl over a range at least from 1°

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to 70°C. This result is in partial conflict with the re-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sults of others on some austenitic steels. The conflict

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is more definite at 1°C, since Horvath and Uhlig (1)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: found that molybdenum had a detrimental effect on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pitting potentials of an austenitic stainless steel series

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in 0.1M NaCl at 0°C. The small differences in experi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mental conditions and technique do not appear suffi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cient to explain a reversal in direction of pitting poten-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tial change with molybdenum content. Thus, the effect

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of molybdenum may be different in austenite than it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is in ferrite even though there is no obvious rationaliz-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ation for the difference. These same considerations also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: apply to the difference in molybdenum effect on aus-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tenite and ferrite tested in NaBr.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: There is less obvious conflict in the behavior of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: molybdenum-containing steels at higher temperatures

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in NaCl. The previously reported results (2) were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: obtained by counting pits formed at constant current

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: density. This involved driving the potential beyond

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that required to produce pitting without determining

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: any pitting or breakthrough potential. It is quite pos-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sible that the number of pits found in this manner

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: does not correlate at all with pitting potentials as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: measured in the present work.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Conclusions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In fully annealed (815°C) 18% Cr ferritic stainless

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: steels, molybdenum additions up to the limit of solid

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: solubility increase pitting potentials. This is true over

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the entire temperature range studied i.e., 1°-70°C in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1M NaCl and 1°-45°C in 1M NaBr. Heat-treatments

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that sensitize the steels to intergranular corrosion also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: drastically lower the pitting potential.
